svg.text: T3 INSTITUTIONAL UNIT — 60,000 L, SCHOOL / CYCLONE SHELTER
400 users · 600 m² roof · full treatment train · 20-day emergency reserve in shelter mode.
Slow sand filtration is what makes institutional rainwater genuinely safe for children: it removes protozoal cysts (Cryptosporidium, Giardia) that chlorine alone does not.
Chlorine is a final barrier and a residual, not a primary treatment. Do not delete the filters to save capital cost.
RCC raft 250 mm · 2 layers Ø12 @150 · waterbar
Wall 200 mm, water-retaining mix, crystalline waterproofing plus food-grade epoxy to the internal face. Roof slab with 2 sealed, lockable,
insect-screened manholes. Hoop tension at base 1.25 MPa, carried by Ø12 @150. Wind: overturning FoS 1.8 at 72 m/s gust before anchorage.
Top the tank up from pre-landfall rain, or run the hand pump. If it is under 70 % full, fill it first and seal afterwards.
All manholes sealed and bolted. Tapstands lashed down. Ladder removed so it cannot become a projectile.
Drinking and cooking only: 5 L/person/day. Hygiene water comes from the shelter pond or PSF, never from this tank.
If relief water arrives, stop drawing from this tank and keep it as the fallback. Re-test the water before reopening.
At 400 people x 5 L/day, a 60,000 L tank gives 30 days of drinking water with no resupply — the most valuable thing this building can hold.
1 named teacher + 1 support staff, trained, named on a board
Pre-filter media replaced; SSF sand scraped when head loss > 0.4 m
2 trained people, ladder + rope + second person outside
0.2–0.5 mg/L at the furthest tap; logged on a board
E. coli 0/100 mL at tank and at tap
3 months of O&M cost held in the school account
Shelter-mode drill with students and committee
